title: GPUs & Accelerators
summary: Why chips built from thousands of simple cores beat a CPU at some jobs and lose badly at others.

blocks.markdown:
A **GPU** (Graphics Processing Unit) trades a few powerful cores for thousands of small, simple ones.

- CPUs optimize for **latency** — finish one task fast.
- GPUs optimize for **throughput** — finish huge numbers of similar tasks per second.
- That's why GPUs power graphics and ML training: "do the same thing to a million items" work.
- They're one member of a bigger family: **accelerators**, chips built for one job, not every job.

**Latency** is how long one task takes start to finish. **Throughput** is how many tasks finish per second overall.

- A CPU core is built to cut latency: big caches, branch prediction, out-of-order execution — all spent making one instruction stream fast.
- A GPU core is built to cut cost-per-task: strip out that machinery, pack thousands of tiny cores, and hide slowness by running many tasks at once.
- Neither is "faster" in general — they're optimized for different questions.

Same silicon budget, opposite bets.

| Trait | CPU | GPU |
|---|---|---|
| Core count | Few (4-64) | Thousands |
| Core design | Complex, deep pipeline | Simple, shallow |
| Best at | Branchy, sequential code | Uniform, data-parallel code |

A CPU core does a lot per instruction; a GPU wins by doing a little, many times over, in parallel.

blocks.subTitle: Why simple cores add up
blocks.markdown:
Fewer transistors per core means far more cores fit on the same chip.

Each GPU core is weaker alone, but hundreds of times more of them run in parallel.

blocks.sectionTitle: SIMT: how a GPU runs code
blocks.markdown:
GPUs execute with **SIMT** (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads): one instruction is broadcast to a group of threads, each applying it to its own data.

- The group is a **warp** (NVIDIA) or **wavefront** (AMD) — typically 32 threads moving in lockstep.
- Code looks like ordinary per-thread logic; hardware runs the whole warp on one instruction underneath.
- The GPU take on [simd-vector-processing](simd-vector-processing), at much larger scale.

blocks.sectionTitle: SIMT: how a GPU runs code
blocks.subTitle: Warp divergence
blocks.markdown:
A warp shares one instruction, so an `if` that splits threads down different paths causes **divergence**.

- The hardware runs *both* branches in turn, masking off threads that don't apply to each one.
- Threads that took the other path just sit idle and wait.
- The more a warp's threads disagree on which branch to take, the more wasted cycles pile up.

A GPU is usually a separate chip with its own memory, so a program deals with two spaces:

- **Host** memory — regular RAM, owned by the CPU.
- **Device** memory — the GPU's own memory, built for very **high bandwidth** (moving huge blocks of data per second) rather than low latency.
- Data must be explicitly copied host to device before the GPU can touch it, and results copied back after.

blocks.subTitle: The PCIe bottleneck
blocks.markdown:
That host-device copy travels over **PCIe**, a link far slower than either memory's internal bandwidth.

- Copying data to the GPU, running one tiny kernel, and copying back can cost more time than the computation itself.
- Rule of thumb: only offload work large and parallel enough that the compute time dwarfs the transfer time.
- Keeping data resident on the GPU across many operations amortizes that one-time transfer cost.

GPUs win when work is **regular** and **data-parallel**: the same operation, repeated over a huge, independent dataset.

- Matrix multiply, image filters, physics steps, neural network layers.
- Thousands of cores stay busy because every thread does near-identical work with little branching.
- Example: multiplying two large matrices maps one output cell to one thread — millions of near-identical, independent threads.

GPUs lose when work is **branchy** or **serial**: each step depends on the last, or threads take wildly different paths.

- Parsing text, walking a linked list, running a database query planner.
- Simple cores have no deep pipeline or branch predictor to hide that, and divergence wastes warp lanes.
- Here a CPU's few strong cores simply finish faster.

blocks.subTitle: TPU
blocks.markdown:
A **TPU** (Tensor Processing Unit) is Google's chip built for one thing: the matrix multiplications behind machine learning.

- It skips general-purpose flexibility for a grid of multiply-add units wired specifically for that math.
- Narrower than a GPU, but faster and more power-efficient for the ML workloads it targets.
- Part of a wider trend covered in [domain-specific-architectures](domain-specific-architectures): give up generality to win on one job.

blocks.subTitle: FPGA & ASIC
blocks.markdown:
Two more ways to trade flexibility for speed.

| Chip | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| FPGA | Reprogrammable circuits — flexible, slower and pricier per op than a fixed chip |
| ASIC | Custom-built for one exact task — fastest and cheapest at scale, fixed forever |

**FPGA** (Field-Programmable Gate Array) can be rewired after manufacturing. **ASIC** (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) cannot — the design is baked in.

**Heterogeneous computing** means combining different kinds of processors in one system, each handling the work it's best at.

- CPU: control flow, I/O, branchy logic, orchestrating everything else.
- GPU/TPU/ASIC: the narrow, parallel, high-volume slice of the workload.
- A phone's chip already does this: CPU cores, a GPU, and an ML accelerator side by side, each fed the work it fits.

Common mistakes:

- **"More cores always means faster."** Only if the work is truly parallel — branchy code on a GPU can lose to a CPU.
- **"Moving data to the GPU is free."** The PCIe transfer often costs more than the compute it enables.
- **"An ASIC is just a faster GPU."** It's narrower, not faster in general — it only wins on the exact task it was built for.

blocks.subTitle: CPU vs GPU — when to use which
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: CPU vs GPU — when would you pick each?**

CPU when the work is sequential, branchy, or latency-sensitive — control logic, parsing, one request at a time. GPU when the same operation repeats over a large, independent dataset — rendering, matrix math, ML training. Real systems use both: CPU orchestrates, GPU crunches the parallel part.

blocks.subTitle: What is SIMT / a warp
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is SIMT, and what is a warp?**

SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) broadcasts one instruction to a group of threads that each run it on their own data. That group — typically 32 threads — is a warp. It looks like normal threaded code, but the hardware executes the whole warp in lockstep, SIMD-style underneath.

blocks.subTitle: Why GPUs struggle with branches
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why are GPUs bad at branchy code?**

A warp's threads share one instruction stream. If an `if` sends threads down different paths, the hardware runs both paths serially, masking off the threads that don't belong to each one — so divergent branches waste cycles instead of running in parallel.

blocks.subTitle: What is a TPU
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a TPU, and how does it differ from a GPU?**

A TPU is a chip built specifically for the matrix multiplications in machine learning, with no general-purpose graphics or compute flexibility. It trades the GPU's broader programmability for higher speed and efficiency on that one workload.

blocks.subTitle: What is heterogeneous computing
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is heterogeneous computing?**

Running a workload across different kinds of processors — CPU, GPU, TPU, ASIC — each handling the slice of work it's best suited for, instead of forcing everything onto one general-purpose chip. See [multicore-multiprocessing](multicore-multiprocessing) for the same idea applied within identical cores.
